root_tweet.text: Someone pointed me to this page on the website of the Western Australian government, and I challenge you to find a MORE attention-getting heading on that site. [1/?] https://t.co/Xm7MHOLka7

children.text:
In case you can’t see it, the page heading is “Public Health Act 2016 (WA) – Instrument of Authorisation – Authorisation to Supply or Administer a Poison [SARS-COV-2 (COVID-19) VACCINE – Australian Defence Force] (No.2) 2021”.

As I said, attention-getting.

TL;DR: Seems like the Australian government uses, for ANY substance that gets regulated because of potential harm, the umbrella term "poisons". This includes things like aspirin, folic acid, and iodine - things no one would class as "poisons" in the everyday sense.

Anyone claiming "This substance must be harmful to us, because the Aus gov't classifies it as a 'poison'!" has only proved they don't know the faintest thing about how the Aus gov't classifies substances, and shouldn't be listened to.
Obviously there’s an explanation, but what is it? I thought this was a good opportunity to show how I research something like this, to figure out what it does and doesn’t mean.

I try to start by thinking of at least two POSSIBLE explanations. Why two? Because the natural tendency we’re all born with, called confirmation bias, is to come up with only ONE explanation - and then process EVERYTHING we see thereafter through that lens.

The first, most obvious explanation is that, in this document, the WA government is using the word “poison” in its everyday sense - meaning a substance that, by its nature, harms creatures exposed to it.

If this explanation is true, it means that the WA government actively plotted to cause harm to its own citizens - and then decided, for NO GOOD REASON, to announce that scandalous intent to the entire Internet and keep the evidence of plotting in plain view for months.

This teaches an important lesson. The “first, most obvious explanation” frequently has MASSIVE, insurmountable problems that make it HIGHLY unlikely. But we’re still going to keep this explanation in mind, calling it the “‘poison’ as we use that term”, or PAWUTT explanation.

A second possible explanation is that this LEGAL DOCUMENT is using legal language that the general public (i.e., US) isn’t familiar with. If you remove ONE WORD, “poison”, from the document, suddenly it looks dry and bureaucratic, not lurid and sinister.

Is this a likely explanation? It sure is. Every profession has “terms of art” which have one meaning to the general public but a different meaning to the professionals. Our second hypothesis is that “poison” as it’s used in the government notice is a “term of art”: PIATOA.
But just because PIATOA is the more likely of the two explanations I’ve thought of DOESN’T mean it must be right. So I see if I can find anything to confirm or deny this hypothesis.

My first avenue of investigation is to search the web for the phrase used in the notice: “to supply or administer a poison”. It sounds like “boilerplate” language common in legal writing, which would make sense if PIATOA.

Unfortunately, this search isn’t fruitful. It doesn’t produce what I hoped for: notices of authorization to administer benign substances like saline solution, aspirin, blood plasma, etc., that TERM them “poison”. Such notices would debunk PAWUTT.

Instead, the search brings up instances of people on social media finding the https://t.co/ZybNj50UNG page in question and freaking TF out. This is not evidence for PAWUTT, BTW. I can find plenty of people on social media insisting that the Earth is flat. That don’t make it flat.

So I try a new search avenue. The page heading that has so many alarmed begins with “Public Health Act 2016 (WA)”, so why not look there? I search for the term “administer” in the text of the Act at https://t.co/hPXuW67da5 .

I readily find the following:

“197. Chief Health Officer may authorise persons to administer, manufacture, supply or prescribe poisons
“(1) In this section — 
**poison** —

“(a) until the commencement of the Medicines and Poisons Act 2014 section 3, has the meaning given in the Poisons Act 1964 section 5(1); and
“(b) after the commencement of the Medicines and Poisons Act 2014 section 3, has the meaning given in that section.”

DEFINITELY a nail in the coffin for PAWUTT; there would be *no need* to specify the meaning of “poison” if it was the meaning everyone uses. Still, it seems unusual to use “poison” in this context, so let’s keep investigating.

https://t.co/IgXQOPuBqn The Poisons Act of 1964, section 5(1) says “**poison** means any substance included in a Schedule”. https://t.co/j8QeBP8FAZ The Medicine and Poisons Act 2014 section 3 says “**poison** means a substance that is a Schedule 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 poison”.

That’s a bit recursive, but *the very next section* of the latter document spells out what the schedules designate, e.g. “**Schedule 2 — Pharmacy medicines**
Substances, the safe use of which may require advice from a pharmacist and which should be available from a pharmacy ...
... or, where a pharmacy service is not available, from a licensed person.”

How many substances which are “poisons” in the conventional sense of the word are ALSO “pharmacy medicines” whose “safe use” MAY require advice from a pharmacist?? PAWUTT is pretty fricking dead at this point.

I won’t bore you with every detail of how I found the schedules themselves at https://t.co/3d8vot5j8d . Just read it yourself and see that Schedule 2 “poisons” include aspirin, benzocaine, diphenhydramine, folic acid, ibuprofen, iodine, naproxen and paracetamol.

Can we *imagine* scenarios in which those substances are ABUSED to do harm? Sure, but that’s irrelevant. The POINT is that no one would hear “the WA government authorized someone to supply or administer aspirin” and gasp “that’s a Schedule 2 poison! they’re trying to poison us!”

That would be ridiculous.

And it’s equally ridiculous to point to this https://t.co/ZybNj50UNG page on SARS-CoV-2 vaccine and gasp “The vaccine must be harmful!”
Do I know WHY the WA government uses the word “poisons” to describe a WIDE variety of substances, many of which you might use every day of your life rightfully expecting it to do you no harm?

No, I don’t. I wish I did know. But the IMPORTANT point is, THEY DO. Since at least 1964, they’ve used the word “poisons” in a way that CLEARLY includes MUCH more than what the ordinary person considers poisons.
And that’s not at all hard to find out. If you do your research. [end]
